briefing: Brent crude is holding near $105 a barrel as the U.S. and Iran trade claims over whether the Strait of Hormuz is open, and GTA gas is around $1.80 a litre. Mark Carney is rallying in Alberta before Monday's referendum, and Toronto's mayoral race tightens ahead of October 26 after record advance voting. In Washington, six Republican senators have joined Democrats against Trump's Russian diesel deal as the midterms near.
headline: Oil holds near $105; senators push back on Russian diesel deal

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of nuclear talks. The first wave killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, Gulf states and U.S. bases, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. A peace memorandum signed in June briefly reopened shipping, but it fell apart in July when Iran started attacking commercial ships again to press its claim over the strait.
stories.headline: Oil holds near $105 as U.S. and Iran trade claims over Hormuz
stories.impact: This is a big part of why gas and diesel in Ontario stay expensive: GTA regular is forecast around $1.80 a litre on Friday and diesel near $2.65. Diesel feeds straight into grocery and delivery prices, and higher fuel is one reason the Bank of Canada has been cautious about cutting rates.
stories.now: Iran's army chief said early Friday that the strait remains closed, while CENTCOM said commercial traffic continues and more than 19 million barrels of crude moved through it in a single day; CENTCOM also rejected Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) claims that a container ship hit a mine and that U.S. troops were killed in Jordan. The Institute for the Study of War counts at least 24 commercial ships targeted near the strait in two weeks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced more sanctions on Iran-linked financial networks, and Israel's Channel 12 reported unusual military movements inside Iran. In early Asian trade Friday, Brent was about $105.50 and U.S. benchmark WTI about $97.40, after WTI jumped 3% Thursday; physical cargoes (Dated Brent) traded near $130. Kpler shipping data cited by Reuters show Hormuz crude flows averaged about 11.6 million barrels a day in the week to October 13, down from a normal 17.2 million. Traders are also watching whether Washington eases limits on Russia's so-called shadow fleet of tankers, which helped nudge prices lower in early trade.

stories.backstory: The Iran war, and especially attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, pushed oil above $100 a barrel this year. U.S. gas averaged about $2.98 a gallon before the war, and diesel hit a record $6.29 in late September. Wages are rising about 3% a year, slower than prices, so many Americans are falling behind. Rising long-term borrowing costs have also hit stock markets, especially debt-heavy AI companies.
stories.headline: U.S. inflation jumps to 3.7% as gas prices hit records
stories.impact: U.S. bond yields help set Canadian fixed mortgage rates, so GTA homeowners renewing soon could see higher offers. Fuel costs feed into everything from groceries to delivery prices in Ontario.
stories.now: The U.S. consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August and above the 3.6% economists expected. Gasoline jumped 9.1% in the month, and the U.S. average pump price hit a record $4.33 a gallon; core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose to 2.6%. CME Group data showed traders putting about a 44% chance on a quarter-point Fed hike on October 28, up from roughly 20% before the report. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield touched 5.30% earlier this month, its highest since 2002, before easing to about 5.05% Thursday, and the average 30-year mortgage rate rose to 7.56%. White House adviser Kevin Hassett blamed the jump on Houthi attacks on Saudi oil sites.

stories.why: Higher U.S. inflation and interest rates ripple into Canada through borrowing costs, the dollar and trade. It also sharpens the cost-of-living debate three weeks before the midterms.

stories.backstory: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad emergency tariffs in February, but sector tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, copper and lumber stayed. At the first CUSMA review on July 1, the U.S. refused to extend the deal for a full new term, so it now needs annual reviews. Ottawa walked out of talks on August 21, calling Washington's last-minute demands unfair. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on August 22, and Canada matched with counter-tariffs on September 8, plus a $25B support package for affected workers and businesses.
stories.headline: Trump says Canada will end up the 51st state; Ford says never
stories.impact: Tariffs raise prices on some U.S. goods in Canadian stores and squeeze manufacturing jobs in the GTA, Windsor and Hamilton. If you or your family work in autos, steel, logistics or anything that ships to the U.S., this is the story most likely to touch your paycheque.
stories.now: Speaking in Bullhead City, Arizona, on Wednesday, Trump said Canada will end up as the 51st state, argued the U.S. does not need Canada, and again floated renaming Lake Ontario. He pointed to Canada's dairy tariffs and to automakers moving plants to the U.S. Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered that Canada's sovereignty is not for sale. Earlier that day U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra suggested that Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's talk of aiming counter-tariffs at particular U.S. states could look like interference in the November 3 midterms, while Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre toured Michigan arguing for tariff-free auto trade. Separately, a draft joint statement seen by The Canadian Press shows Canada and the European Union planning closer ties on digital security, critical minerals and a proposed fleet of Canadian-built water bombers ahead of a summit at the end of October.

stories.backstory: Premier Danielle Smith announced the referendum in February and added the separation question in May. A yes on that question would not take Alberta out of Canada; it would start a process toward a later, binding referendum. Other questions ask about provincial control over immigration, proof of citizenship to vote, and making provincial law override federal law.
stories.headline: Carney tells Calgary rally to vote like Canada depends on it
stories.impact: Indirect for Ontario, but a strong separatist showing would dominate federal politics and could affect transfer payments and national programs that every province shares.
stories.now: The Prime Minister's Office estimated at least 5,000 people at Thursday night's Calgary rally, where Carney said a vote to leave would bring deep division and uncertainty and warned supporters not to assume the result is settled. Earlier he urged a no on the nine other questions about immigration powers and the Constitution. Premier Danielle Smith, who says she voted to stay, spoke at a $500-a-plate United Conservative Party fundraiser at the same time; her government is spending $4 million on ads for the nine questions, while the federal government is spending about $250,000 on its own ads. On Friday Carney holds a rally in Edmonton and meets business leaders with Smith in Red Deer, while Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Smith both speak at a conservative conference in Calgary. Advance polls close Saturday and voting day is Monday, October 19. An Abacus Data survey taken October 7–13 found 68% of Albertans trust Elections Alberta to count ballots fairly, but only 40% expect both sides to respect the result, and most expect the separation debate to continue after the vote. The Alberta Federation of Labour plans province-wide unity events Saturday and a rally at the legislature Sunday, and the pro-separation Let Alberta Decide group has its own rally planned.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion is in its fifth year. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been trying to coax Moscow back to talks, and reportedly see letting Russian diesel back onto the market as a carrot. European intelligence services warn Russia may take bigger risks against NATO countries in the coming months.
stories.headline: New Russian strikes cut power in Kyiv as Zelenskyy heads to EU summit
stories.impact: Ukrainian hits on Russian refineries can tighten world diesel supply, which matters because diesel already feeds grocery and delivery costs in Ontario. Canada is a NATO member and a major Ukraine backer, so a widening split between Washington and Kyiv affects Ottawa's defence and aid decisions.
stories.now: Ukraine's energy ministry and grid operator Ukrenergo said Russian attacks overnight and Friday morning hit energy facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv, Volyn, Odesa and Rivne regions, with more outages from shelling in at least six other regions. Hourly blackouts apply to all customers in some areas, and Ukrenergo asked people to limit heavy appliance use from 4 p.m. to 10 p.m. as colder weather pushes up demand. Earlier this week strikes on power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv left at least 600,000 people without electricity, and Zelenskyy met NATO chief Mark Rutte on Thursday seeking more air defence. Ukraine has resumed drone strikes on Russian refineries, saying the energy ceasefire Trump announced on October 11 was never honoured. Zelenskyy joins EU leaders in Brussels on Friday to discuss support for Ukraine.

stories.backstory: Chow won a 2023 by-election after John Tory resigned and is now seeking a full term. Bradford, a councillor, is her main challenger. Late-summer polls had Chow around 50% and Bradford near 39%. Big themes are housing costs, traffic, property taxes and the province's moves on bike lanes.
stories.headline: Chow pledges 15,000 youth jobs as Bradford pitches Eglinton East LRT
stories.impact: You get a vote for mayor, ward councillor and school trustee in your own city. Check your municipality's site for your polling station and advance-voting hours.
stories.now: Chow promised 15,000 new youth jobs, a guarantee that 20% of Scarborough East LRT construction jobs go to local residents, and $28 million for youth violence prevention, mentorship and employment programs. Bradford called her campaign out of steam, pledged to push the Eglinton East LRT in his first 100 days with construction starting by 2030, and repeated plans to remove 12 km of red bus lanes in Scarborough. The two also clashed over Bradford's proposed Toronto Water utility, which he says would stay fully public and Chow says could hand control to the province. A record 225,550 Torontonians voted in advance polls; the final televised debate airs on CP24 on October 22 at 7 p.m., and election day is Monday, October 26, with polls open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

stories.backstory: Republicans have controlled both the House and Senate since January 2025, which has let Trump pass his agenda with few checks. Midterms usually go against the president's party, and Trump's approval is lower than at the same point in his first term. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot. A Democratic House could launch investigations and block spending and trade legislation.
stories.headline: Early voting surges and Senate money pours in, 18 days before the midterms
stories.impact: A change in Congress could shift the odds of tariff relief for Ontario's auto, steel and lumber industries. Ottawa's trade strategy is partly being timed around the outcome.
stories.now: Georgia logged more than 180,000 ballots on its first day of early voting, about 55,000 more than in 2022, and North Carolina opened in-person early voting on Thursday. In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico reported raising $64 million in the third quarter against Republican Ken Paxton's $18 million, while Elon Musk's America PAC says it has given $276 million to Republican groups over three months. Trump endorsed Ohio Sen. Jon Husted against Democrat Sherrod Brown and Michigan Republican Mike Rogers, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries previewed a 100-day agenda on living costs, health care and ending tariffs. Polling averages give Democrats a lead of roughly 8 points on the generic ballot (which party voters want in Congress), and Republicans hold the Senate 53–47. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson clashed in a debate in a race rated a toss-up, and the Justice Department sued California over what it says are more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens on voter rolls. The U.S. Postal Service says it will take special steps from October 24 to speed mail ballots. Trump rallies in Dalton, Georgia, on Friday for Republican Rep. Mike Collins against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, and has been publicly blaming others for a possible Republican loss in Texas.

stories.headline: Six Republican senators join Democrats against Trump's Russian diesel deal
stories.summary: A bipartisan group of 12 senators asked Trump on Tuesday to cancel his deal to let Russian diesel reach world markets and to enforce a new Russia sanctions law instead.
stories.now: On October 9 Trump announced that Russia would supply diesel to global markets and his administration temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel. On October 13, twelve senators, six of them Republicans, wrote to urge him to rescind the deal and apply the new law that directs tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil. Retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said there is a legitimate case that the president is not following the law, while Senate Republican whip John Barrasso defended the deal as a balancing act. Reports put the volume at roughly 3 to 5 million tons, and one estimate of about 36 million barrels is under two weeks of U.S. demand. More Republican Senate candidates are now distancing themselves from it on the campaign trail.
stories.backstory: Russia's oil and fuel exports have been under Western sanctions since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, meant to cut the revenue that funds the war. Fuel prices have climbed this year because of the Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Congress recently passed a law directing significant tariffs on the biggest importers of Russian oil, and the diesel deal pulls in the opposite direction.

timeline.event: Western sanctions target Russian oil and fuel after the invasion of Ukraine.

stories.why: It tests whether Republicans in Congress will push back on the White House before the midterms, and it complicates Western pressure on Russia while Ukraine's power grid is being hit.
stories.impact: Diesel prices feed into grocery, trucking and delivery costs in Ontario. Analysts doubt the deal would meaningfully lower pump prices, and it could weaken sanctions pressure that Canada has backed.

stories.backstory: The Houthis, an Iran-aligned movement controlling much of northern Yemen, joined the Iran war in late March by firing at Israel. Since then the fight has widened into a direct Saudi-Houthi confrontation, with Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and on the East-West oil pipeline that Saudi Arabia uses to bypass Hormuz.
stories.headline: Houthi strike on Aden presidential palace kills five; Riyadh airport stays shut
stories.impact: Indirect but real: more disruption to Red Sea shipping means slower and pricier imported goods and another push on fuel prices in Canada.
stories.now: Yemen's health minister raised the toll from Thursday's attack on the al-Maashiq palace in Aden, seat of the Saudi-backed government, to five dead and 16 wounded; the prime minister and cabinet were unharmed. The Houthis say they targeted a Saudi military headquarters there, a claim Reuters could not verify. Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki says the Houthis have launched 20 attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333, plus attacks on Abha airport that killed three, and that coalition jets have destroyed 127 weapons depots and launch sites in Yemen. Riyadh's main airport is to stay closed until the evening of October 17, and more than 3,000 flights from Saudi airports were cancelled or grounded in a week. A Saudi official said the Houthis turned down a proposed meeting in Muscat, Oman, and Riyadh accused Iran of arming and training them. An EU–Gulf summit planned for October 24 in Riyadh has been postponed, and Trump says he is considering joining strikes on the Houthis.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco in 2024. Ottawa approved the deal under the Investment Canada Act on the condition that it keep union jobs and most non-union positions, more than 1,500 in total.
stories.headline: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO calls Ottawa's Stelco threats bullying
stories.impact: Steel layoffs ripple through suppliers and local businesses across the Golden Horseshoe. It also signals how hard Ottawa will push on other foreign-owned plants in Ontario.
stories.now: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told BNN Bloomberg on Thursday that Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's threats amount to bullying and harassment, saying the company did not expect to be treated like a pariah less than two years after buying Stelco. He called the cuts a business decision to concentrate production, says he intends to rehire the workers once trade conditions improve, and denies breaking the commitments made under the Investment Canada Act. Joly says everything is on the table, including forced sale of assets or financial penalties. The steelworkers' local expects 300 to 350 layoffs in Hamilton itself, with more at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, and the Ontario NDP wants Premier Doug Ford to push for public ownership.

stories.backstory: Election workers in the U.S. have faced a sharp rise in threats since 2020, and suspicious packages were sent to officials in at least six states during the 2024 election. Most such powders have turned out to be harmless, but each one forces evacuations, testing and delays. The latest letters arrive as early voting and mail ballot processing ramp up across many states ahead of the midterms.
stories.headline: Letters with white powder sent to U.S. election offices weeks before midterms
stories.impact: There is no direct risk to Ontario, but disruption or disputes over the midterm count could add to U.S. political uncertainty that already weighs on trade talks and markets. Canadians mailing items to U.S. officials are not affected.
stories.now: Election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma received letters holding a white powdery substance, and federal officials intercepted similar letters headed to the secretaries of state in Ohio and New Hampshire. North Carolina election offices also received envelopes with white powder on Thursday, the first day of early voting there; officials said no harmful substance was identified. Three election officials told Votebeat more than 100 letters were mailed nationwide, including to at least one senator and a polling firm. The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service say the investigation is broad but have not identified the substance in the other cases.

stories.backstory: Premier Doug Ford's government passed a 2024 law letting it remove bike lanes on major Toronto roads, arguing they worsen traffic. A lower court ruled in 2025 that the law violated the Charter, but in August a three-judge appeal panel unanimously reversed that.
stories.headline: Third arrest at Bloor bike lane protest as removal work continues
stories.impact: Expect lane restrictions and protests on Bloor West between Royal York and Islington through mid-November, whether you drive, bike or take the bus there. How much this costs is also a live question in the October 26 mayoral vote.
stories.now: Police arrested a woman near Bloor Street West and Lothian Avenue on Thursday for mischief and obstructing police, the third arrest since work began. On Wednesday, a 25-year-old Hamilton woman was charged with mischief and obstructing police, and a 20-year-old Toronto man was charged with mischief and theft after police say he pulled down city signs. Crews are removing about one kilometre of lanes between Islington Avenue and Royal York Road, with work set to run to November 17; Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says the lanes are coming out. A Nanos poll for CP24 and CTV found 74% of Chow supporters back more bike lanes while 74% of Bradford supporters oppose them, and 45% of residents said transportation experts and city staff should decide.

stories.backstory: Omar, who came to the U.S. as a refugee from Somalia, has represented Minneapolis since 2019 and is a frequent target of Trump. The Justice Department has traditionally avoided public steps against candidates within about 60 days of an election. Democrats say the search fits a pattern of the administration using law enforcement against critics; officials say they are following evidence. No charges have been filed.

stories.impact: Little direct effect in Ontario, but it adds to tension heading into midterms that will shape U.S. policy toward Canada.
stories.now: A person briefed on the case told the Associated Press that investigators seized Omar's phone and that a Minnesota grand jury has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, some to her relatives. Homeland Security officers searched her Washington home on Monday, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested the focus is her family's immigration paperwork. D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said there are several investigations, including into Omar's financial disclosures. Omar calls it an attempt to weaponize federal law enforcement against political enemies.

stories.backstory: Ontario Place opened on Toronto's waterfront in 1971. The Ford government's plan includes a privately run spa, a relocated Ontario Science Centre, new parkland and shoreline, a parking garage that will cost taxpayers about $200 million, and a police detachment. The 2023 act exempted the project from some environmental, heritage and municipal noise rules and limited legal challenges. An Ontario judge dismissed the coalition's case in 2024, and the Court of Appeal unanimously upheld that ruling.
stories.headline: Supreme Court hears challenge to Ontario Place law
stories.impact: Construction is under way, so a ruling is unlikely to stop the project quickly, but it could affect how the province uses similar laws for highways, bike lanes and other GTA projects.
stories.now: The Ontario Place Protectors coalition told the Supreme Court of Canada on Thursday that the Rebuilding Ontario Place Act strips superior courts of core powers, such as granting injunctions and damages, that the Constitution protects. It also asks the court to recognize a public trust doctrine that would protect public lands like Ontario Place. The province says the law's immunity is limited, does not make the site lawless, and that the public trust idea has no basis in the record. Several provinces, First Nations, civil liberties and environmental groups are intervening, and a ruling may not come until next year.

sources.title: CP24: Supreme Court hears Ontario Place challenge

stories.summary: Canada's top court is hearing a citizens' group argue that the law clearing the way for Ontario Place's redevelopment unconstitutionally shields the province from the courts.

timeline.event: Ontario judge dismisses the challenge.
Supreme Court agrees to hear the case.
Province confirms ~$200M public parking garage.
Supreme Court hearing.

stories.why: The case could set national limits on how far governments can use legislation to block court review of their projects.
